title: Swing Low, Sweet Chariot
origin: African-American spiritual, Indian Territory / Oklahoma; carried worldwide by the Fisk Jubilee Singers

pd.detail: Traditional spiritual attributed to Wallace Willis before 1865; in print and on record by 1909 with the Fisk Jubilee Singers, long out of copyright in the United States.
pd.sourceEdition: Traditional lead sheet in D major as printed in the John C. Campbell Folk School Song Book (anonymous, melody and chords only)
pd.notes: This block covers the MUSIC only; the words carry their own separate basis in each section's lyrics.pd. The tune is famous through many modern covers and one rugby-terrace arrangement; what is encoded here is the traditional melody, not any modern arrangement. Chords are a bar-granular reduction: the printed chart moves IV and V7 mid-bar in places and v1 folds each bar into its primary chord.

notes: Common time throughout, no meter reduction needed. The verse pickup (scale degree 3) lives on the last beat of the chorus, so chorus into verse lands the famous upbeat; the chorus itself begins on the downbeat and needs no pickup.

pd.detail: Anonymous African-American spiritual text, sung before 1865 and first set down in print by the Fisk Jubilee Singers' collectors in the 1870s. The printings credit no author; the oral attribution to Wallace Willis, a nineteenth-century freedman of the Choctaw Nation, is undocumented and would clear on his death date in any case, so the words are free on either reading. Words first printed in the United States, so no foreign-publication term applies.
pd.sourceEdition: Marsh, J. B. T., 'The Story of the Jubilee Singers: With Their Songs', Boston, 1880

lyrics.notes: One refrain stanza; the chorus sings the same words on every occurrence. Eye-dialect spellings of the 1880 printing are normalised to standard spelling; no words are added, dropped or reordered.

stanzas.text: Coming for to carry me home,
Coming for to carry me home.

lyrics.notes: Stanzas 1 and 2 of the 1880 printing; the two later stanzas it carries are omitted only to keep the form playable, not for content. Eye-dialect spellings are normalised to standard spelling; no words are added, dropped or reordered. Each stanza's odd lines run across two bars, so line 1 covers bars 0-1 and line 3 covers bars 4-5; the pickup note that opens each of those lines sits on the last beat of the preceding bar.

stanzas.text: I looked over Jordan, and what did I see,
Coming for to carry me home,
A band of angels coming after me,
Coming for to carry me home.
If you get there before I do,
Coming for to carry me home,
Tell all my friends I'm coming too,
Coming for to carry me home.
